Fundamentals, explained

What Is Debt Safety?

Whether a company can handle its debt — or whether it's one bad quarter away from trouble.

So what is it, exactly?

Picture this: two neighbors earn the same salary. One has a small mortgage and no other loans. The other has a big mortgage, two car payments, and three maxed-out credit cards. Same income — but let one of them lose a job for three months, and you know exactly which household is in trouble. Companies are no different.

The most common way to size up a company's debt is the debt-to-equity ratio: total debt divided by shareholders' equity. A ratio of 0.5 means 50 cents of debt for every dollar of the owners' money. A ratio of 2.0 means the company owes twice what its owners have put in.

Why should you care?

Because debt is a magnifier. In good times, borrowed money boosts returns and everyone looks brilliant. In bad times, the interest payments keep coming whether or not the customers do — and a heavily indebted company can go from healthy to desperate in a single downturn. Debt doesn't cause the storm, but it decides who survives it.

Some debt is perfectly sensible — companies borrow to build factories and fund growth, just like families borrow to buy homes. The question is never whether a company has debt. It's whether the debt is sized to the business, or the business is shackled to the debt.

Debt Safety is check 7 of 8 on every StockSense report card — the Manageable Debt check. Here's what the row looks like in the app:

Manageable Debt (Debt Safety) Can the company comfortably manage its debt load?
Solid
The grading scale
StrongDebt-to-equity below 0.5 — the balance sheet is clean
SolidDebt-to-equity of 0.5–1.5 — manageable but worth watching
WeakDebt-to-equity above 1.5 — heavy borrowing, higher risk

Let's make it real

Imagine two companies that each hold $100 million of shareholders' equity. Company A carries $30 million in debt. Company B carries $220 million. Same size on the surface — very different balance sheets underneath.

Company A $30M debt ÷ $100M equity
0.3
Light debt load — plenty of room to ride out a rough year.
Company B $220M debt ÷ $100M equity
2.2
Owes more than twice its equity — the lenders come first.

When business is booming, Company B's borrowed money might even make it look like the star. But profits go to shareholders only after lenders get paid — and Company B has a long line of lenders. Debt safety asks the unglamorous question that matters most when things go wrong.
